https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/1-the-end.jpg?&fit=crop&w=1600&h=900
Image via Marvel Comics

Rogue and Gambit’s relationship has never been simple when it comes to touch. For years, something most couples take for granted carried a risk for them. Writer Kelly Thompson explored what that meant for their marriage in Mr. & Mrs. X, especially as Rogue worked to understand and control her powers.

Thompson’s upcoming Universal Monsters: The Bride of Frankenstein Lives is a very different kind of story. Its central character has only just entered the world, and almost every physical experience she has is frightening or painful. When someone finally touches her gently, that does not mean she wants to be touched at all.

Speaking with Collider's Hannah Hunt, Thompson said the tension around touch in the new series is one of its clearest connections to her work on Rogue and Gambit. Asked whether writing the X-Men couple taught her anything she brought to the Bride, Thompson pointed to the “push and the pull” of wanting closeness while having reason to fear it. "I think the touch thing is probably the number one thing," Thompson said.

You are the one shouting at the screen because the characters are not listening. You

The Conjuring

Your nightmare is not really about you. It is about the people
asleep down the hall, and the feeling that whatever is here is not interested in leaving.

The Conjuring films are domestic horror. The house, the family, the perfectly ordinary
room that quietly stops feeling ordinary.

Your instinct is to get everybody into one room. Your fear is protective rather than

This is the one franchise where belief is the weapon. The people who come through it are
the ones who are not alone and refuse to be.

Whatever is here did not come for you. It came for the household, and you are the one
standing in the hallway.

Rogue’s Powers Helped Kelly Thompson Explore the Danger of Touch
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/umbrideoffrank_01_covera_rgb.jpg?q=49&fit=crop&w=750&dpr=2
Image via Skybound

In the first issue, a man named West believes the Bride is his missing wife, Elise. The warmth of his touch stands apart from everything else she has experienced, but Thompson and artist Mattia De Iulis wanted their embrace to feel uncomfortable. Thompson said another artist might have made the moment beautiful. De Iulis understood why it needed to look “horribly awkward” instead. The Bride has just survived violence, fire, and a river. Thompson said she would have no reason to welcome someone reaching for her, however kind he might appear.

That distinction matters throughout a story about a woman learning what her body can do while other people arrive with expectations of what it means to them. Thompson said Rogue’s powers make similar questions unusually literal. As a teenager, Rogue was her favorite character, though she could not fully explain why at the time. Looking back, Thompson sees something beyond the tragedy of Rogue being unable to touch people safely: there was also relief in knowing she could stop them from touching her. Thompson said:
“Part of that was about safety, part of that was about Rogue not being able to be touched, and while that was tragic, there was also relief in it."

She later explored those feelings in Mr. & Mrs. X as Rogue confronted what control over her powers could mean for her relationship with Gambit. The Bride is not Rogue, and Thompson said her experience is less literal, but both characters must decide where their boundaries lie for themselves. The Bride has yet to learn what makes her different from other women, let alone what she wants from anyone who comes close to her. That makes the connection more interesting than a shared reluctance to be touched. For Rogue, touch has long been bound up with both danger and the possibility of intimacy. The Bride is only beginning to understand either one.
